title: Caching
description: A cache keeps frequently-accessed data in a fast store (memory, Redis, CDN) so reads avoid a slower source of truth. Caches trade freshness for speed and are the single highest-leverage lever for read-heavy systems.
example: Redis in front of Postgres for user sessions; CDN caching static assets and API responses.
keyPoints: Cache-aside (lazy): app checks cache, on miss reads DB and populates. Most common.
Write-through: write to cache and DB together, consistent but slower writes.
Write-back: write to cache, flush to DB async, fast but can lose data on crash.
Eviction policies: LRU (default), LFU, FIFO, TTL-based expiry.
summary: Store hot data in a fast layer to cut latency and offload the database.
tradeoffs: Stale reads: cached data can lag the DB, set TTLs or invalidate on write.
Thundering herd: many misses hit the DB at once, use request coalescing / locks.
Cache stampede on expiry, jitter TTLs or refresh-ahead.
whenToUse: Read-heavy workloads, expensive queries, repeated identical requests, hot keys.

title: Load Balancing
description: A load balancer distributes incoming requests across a pool of backend servers, removing single points of failure and enabling horizontal scale. It also performs health checks and can terminate TLS.
example: AWS ALB spreading HTTPS requests across an autoscaling group; NGINX in front of app servers.
keyPoints: L4 (transport) balances by IP/port, fast, protocol-agnostic.
L7 (application) balances by URL/header/cookie, smarter routing, more overhead.
Algorithms: round-robin, least-connections, weighted, IP-hash (sticky).
Health checks remove unhealthy nodes automatically.
summary: Spread traffic across many servers for scale and availability.
tradeoffs: Sticky sessions pin users to a server, simpler but hurts even distribution and failover.
The LB itself must be made HA (active-passive pair, DNS/anycast).
whenToUse: Any service running more than one instance; anywhere you need horizontal scale or zero-downtime deploys.

title: Database Indexing
description: An index is a secondary data structure (usually a B-tree) that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table. Indexes turn O(n) scans into O(log n) lookups at the cost of extra storage and slower writes.
example: Index on users(email) for login lookups; composite (user_id, created_at) for a user timeline.
keyPoints: B-tree indexes serve equality and range queries and keep data sorted.
Hash indexes serve exact-match only, O(1), no ranges.
Composite indexes follow the left-prefix rule, order of columns matters.
Covering index: query answered entirely from the index, no table lookup.
summary: Trade write speed and storage for dramatically faster reads.
tradeoffs: Every index slows INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE and consumes storage.
Over-indexing bloats writes; under-indexing causes full scans.
Low-cardinality columns (booleans) rarely benefit from indexing.
whenToUse: Columns used in WHERE, JOIN, ORDER BY on large tables; foreign keys.

title: Sharding / Partitioning
description: Sharding horizontally partitions data across multiple database instances so each holds a subset. It is how you scale writes and storage past a single machine, at the cost of cross-shard queries and rebalancing complexity.
example: Shard users by hash(user_id) across 16 Postgres instances; shard tweets by user_id.
keyPoints: Shard key choice is everything, it determines hotspots and query fan-out.
Hash sharding spreads evenly but kills range queries.
Range sharding keeps ranges together but risks hot shards.
Consistent hashing minimizes data movement when adding/removing shards.
summary: Split one dataset across many machines when it no longer fits or is too hot for one.
tradeoffs: Cross-shard joins and transactions are hard or impossible.
Rebalancing / resharding is operationally painful.
Hot shards from a skewed key (celebrity problem) undo the benefit.
whenToUse: When a single DB can no longer hold the data or serve the write throughput.

title: Replication & Consistency
description: Replication keeps copies of data on multiple nodes. Synchronous replication is consistent but slow; asynchronous is fast but can serve stale reads and lose recent writes on failover. This is where consistency models live.
example: Postgres primary + read replicas; DynamoDB quorum reads/writes across 3 AZs.
keyPoints: Single-leader: writes to leader, reads from replicas. Simple, most common.
Multi-leader / leaderless (Dynamo): higher availability, conflict resolution needed.
Strong vs eventual consistency; read-your-writes and monotonic-read guarantees.
Quorum: W + R > N gives strong consistency in leaderless systems.
summary: Copy data to multiple nodes for availability and read scale, trading off consistency.
tradeoffs: Async replication lag → stale reads and possible data loss on failover.
Sync replication → higher write latency and reduced availability.
whenToUse: Read scaling, high availability, geographic distribution, disaster recovery.

title: Message Queues
description: A message queue (or log) lets a producer hand off work to be processed later by consumers. It absorbs traffic spikes, decouples services, and enables retries, the backbone of async and event-driven systems.
example: Kafka ingesting clickstream events; SQS buffering image-processing jobs.
keyPoints: Queue (SQS/RabbitMQ): message consumed once, then deleted.
Log (Kafka): durable ordered log, consumers track their own offset, replayable.
Delivery semantics: at-most-once, at-least-once (needs idempotency), exactly-once (hard).
Backpressure and dead-letter queues for poison messages.
summary: Decouple producers from consumers with an async buffer for durability and load-smoothing.
tradeoffs: At-least-once delivery means consumers must be idempotent.
Adds operational complexity and end-to-end latency.
Ordering guarantees usually only hold within a partition.
whenToUse: Spiky workloads, async jobs, decoupling services, event streaming, buffering writes.

title: CAP Theorem
description: CAP states that a distributed system can guarantee at most two of Consistency, Availability, and Partition-tolerance. Since network partitions are unavoidable, the real choice under partition is CP (reject requests to stay consistent) vs AP (stay available, serve possibly-stale data).
example: Banking ledger → CP. Shopping cart / social feed → AP.
keyPoints: Partitions WILL happen, so you pick C or A when they do.
CP systems: reject/stall on partition (e.g. HBase, ZooKeeper, etcd).
AP systems: keep serving, reconcile later (e.g. Cassandra, DynamoDB default).
PACELC extends it: even without partitions, trade Latency vs Consistency.
summary: Under a network partition you must choose consistency or availability, not both.
tradeoffs: CP sacrifices availability during partitions.
AP sacrifices consistency (stale/conflicting reads).
whenToUse: Framing any data-store choice; deciding failure behavior for a stateful service.

title: Consistent Hashing
description: Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a hash ring; each key belongs to the next node clockwise. When a node joins or leaves, only the keys in its arc move, versus naive modulo hashing which remaps almost everything.
example: Memcached client sharding; Cassandra/DynamoDB partitioning; a distributed cache fleet.
keyPoints: Hash ring: keys go to the next node clockwise.
Virtual nodes (vnodes) smooth out uneven load across physical nodes.
Adding/removing a node reassigns only ~K/N keys.
summary: Map keys to nodes so adding/removing a node moves only ~1/N of the keys.
tradeoffs: Without vnodes, load can be uneven and failures cause hotspots.
More complex than modulo hashing to implement and reason about.
whenToUse: Distributed caches, sharded databases, load balancers with sticky routing.

title: Rate Limiting
description: Rate limiting rejects or delays requests that exceed a quota, protecting backends from overload and abuse. The algorithm choice controls burst behavior and memory cost.
example: Redis token bucket keyed by API key; per-IP login throttling.
keyPoints: Token bucket: tokens refill at a rate, allows bursts up to bucket size. Most popular.
Leaky bucket: smooths output to a fixed rate.
Fixed window: simple but allows 2x burst at window edges.
Sliding window log/counter: accurate, more memory.
summary: Cap how many requests a client can make to protect the system and ensure fairness.
tradeoffs: Distributed rate limiting needs shared state (Redis) → adds latency.
Fixed windows have edge bursts; sliding windows cost more memory.
whenToUse: Public APIs, login endpoints, expensive operations, per-user fairness, abuse prevention.

title: CDN
description: A Content Delivery Network caches content on geographically distributed edge servers so users fetch from a nearby POP instead of the origin. It slashes latency for static assets and offloads the origin.
example: CloudFront/Cloudflare serving a SPA bundle and images worldwide.
keyPoints: Pull CDN: fetches from origin on first request, then caches at the edge.
Push CDN: you upload content to the CDN ahead of time.
Cache-control headers and TTLs govern freshness; use versioned URLs for busting.
Modern CDNs also cache API responses and run edge compute.
summary: Serve content from edge locations near users to cut latency and origin load.
tradeoffs: Cache invalidation across edges is slow, prefer versioned/immutable URLs.
Dynamic/personalized content benefits less from a CDN.
whenToUse: Static assets (JS/CSS/images/video), global user base, high read volume.

title: Design a URL Shortener
coreEntities: URL { short_code (PK), long_url, user_id, created_at, expires_at }

deepDives.title: Unique code generation at scale
deepDives.content: A single auto-increment is a bottleneck/SPOF. Use a key-generation service that hands out ranges (e.g. each app server pre-allocates a block of 1000 counter values), or use a distributed counter (Redis INCR / ZooKeeper / a ticket server). Base62-encode the number for a compact code. Pre-generating keys offline into a "available keys" table is another common answer.

deepDives.title: Read scaling & latency
deepDives.content: Redirects dominate traffic. Cache short_code→long_url in Redis (LRU), hit rate is very high because a small set of links go viral. Add a CDN so popular redirects are served at the edge. The DB (DynamoDB/Cassandra) is partitioned by short_code, giving even load and O(1) lookups.

deepDives.title: 301 vs 302
deepDives.content: 301 (permanent) lets browsers cache the redirect, reducing load, but then you lose click analytics and can never change the target. 302 (temporary) routes every click through your servers, enabling analytics at higher cost. Most shorteners use 302 for this reason.

estimations: ~100M new URLs/day → ~1160 writes/sec.
Reads at 100:1 → ~116k reads/sec.
Storage: 100M/day × 5yr × ~500 bytes ≈ 100 TB.
62^7 (a-zA-Z0-9, 7 chars) ≈ 3.5 trillion codes, plenty.
functionalReqs: Create a short URL from a long URL (optionally a custom alias).
Redirect a short URL to the original long URL.
Optional: expiration, click analytics.
highLevelDesign: Client → Load Balancer → stateless API servers → database (key-value store like DynamoDB, keyed by short_code). On create, generate a unique code and store the mapping. On read, look up the code and return a 301/302 redirect. Put a cache (Redis) in front of the DB for hot codes, and a CDN/edge for the redirect path. Code generation options: (1) base62-encode an auto-increment counter (needs a distributed counter like a Redis INCR or a range-allocation service), or (2) hash the URL and take the first 7 chars (handle collisions by retrying). Prefer the counter approach for guaranteed uniqueness without collision checks.
nonFunctionalReqs: Highly available (redirects must not fail).
Redirect latency < ~100ms.
Read-heavy: ~100:1 read:write ratio.
Short codes are not guessable (optional).
problem: Design a service like bit.ly / TinyURL that shortens long URLs into short codes and redirects users when they visit a short link.
summary: TinyURL: turn long URLs into short codes and redirect. The classic warm-up.

title: Design a Rate Limiter
apiDesign: Internal middleware: allow(client_id) → { allowed: bool, remaining, retry_after }
coreEntities: Counter { key = client_id + window, count, expiry }

deepDives.title: Algorithm choice
deepDives.content: Token bucket allows controlled bursts and is memory-cheap (2 numbers/client). Sliding-window counter is more accurate at window edges but costs more. Fixed window is simplest but permits a 2x burst straddling the boundary. State the trade-off and pick token bucket unless strict smoothing is required (then leaky bucket).

deepDives.title: Race conditions & atomicity
deepDives.content: Read-modify-write on the counter from many servers races. Solve with an atomic Redis Lua script or INCR + EXPIRE so check-and-decrement is one operation. Otherwise two concurrent requests can both see tokens available and both pass.

deepDives.title: Availability & failure mode
deepDives.content: If Redis is down, decide fail-open (allow traffic, prioritize availability) vs fail-closed (reject, prioritize protection). Usually fail-open for user-facing APIs. Use a Redis cluster / replicas for HA. Local in-memory counters with periodic sync reduce Redis load but weaken accuracy.

estimations: If 10k req/sec across fleet, the limiter store must handle ~10k+ ops/sec.
Per-client counter is tiny (a few bytes), memory is not the constraint; op throughput is.
functionalReqs: Allow or reject a request based on a per-client quota (e.g. 100 req/min).
Return remaining quota and retry-after info.
Configurable limits per client/endpoint tier.
highLevelDesign: Rate limiting runs as middleware in each API server (or at the API gateway) backed by a shared, fast store, Redis, holding per-client counters. On each request the server runs the algorithm against Redis (ideally in a single atomic Lua script to avoid races) and allows or returns 429. Token bucket is the usual choice: store {tokens, last_refill} per client, refill lazily on read. Centralizing state in Redis keeps all servers consistent; the gateway placement keeps rejected traffic away from backends.
nonFunctionalReqs: Very low added latency (< a few ms).
Highly available, must not become a SPOF that blocks all traffic.
Accurate enough; consistent across the server fleet.
problem: Design a rate limiter that restricts each client (by API key or IP) to N requests per time window, working correctly across many API servers.
summary: A distributed service that caps requests per client across a fleet of servers.

title: Design a Chat / Messaging Service
coreEntities: Message { id, chat_id, sender_id, body, created_at, status }
Inbox / delivery state per user per chat.

deepDives.title: Delivery guarantees & ordering
deepDives.content: Use per-chat sequence numbers or client-generated message IDs for idempotency and ordering. At-least-once delivery + dedup by message ID gives effectively-once. ACKs drive the sent→delivered→read state machine; unacked messages are retried on reconnect.

deepDives.title: Connection management at scale
deepDives.content: 100M+ concurrent sockets need many gateway servers. A registry (Redis) maps user→server so senders can route. On disconnect, the registry entry expires. Sticky routing keeps a user on one server; on failover the client reconnects and re-registers.

deepDives.title: Offline delivery & push
deepDives.content: If a recipient is offline, persist to their per-user inbox and trigger APNs/FCM push. On reconnect the client pulls undelivered messages by cursor. This is why a durable store + queue sits behind the real-time path.

deepDives.title: Group fan-out
deepDives.content: Small groups: fan out on write to each member's inbox. Very large groups/channels: fan out on read (members pull) to avoid write amplification, the classic push vs pull trade-off, same as social feeds.

estimations: 500M DAU, ~40 msgs/user/day → ~20B msgs/day → ~230k msgs/sec.
Persistent connections: potentially 100M+ concurrent WebSocket connections.
Storage: 20B × ~200 bytes/day ≈ 4 TB/day.
functionalReqs: Send/receive messages in 1:1 and group chats in real time.
Delivery + read receipts; message history.
Online/last-seen presence.
highLevelDesign: Clients hold a persistent WebSocket to a fleet of stateful Chat/Gateway servers (behind an L4 LB). A connection registry (Redis) maps user_id → which gateway server holds their socket. To send: sender's gateway persists the message (Cassandra, partitioned by chat_id), then looks up each recipient's gateway and forwards over their socket; if offline, the message waits in durable storage and a push notification is sent. Presence is tracked via heartbeats in Redis with TTL. Group messages fan out to each member. A message queue (Kafka) decouples persistence, fan-out, and push-notification workers.
nonFunctionalReqs: Low latency delivery (< ~200ms) for online users.
Highly available and durable, no lost messages.
Scale to hundreds of millions of connections.
problem: Design a real-time messaging system supporting 1:1 and group chats, online presence, and delivery/read receipts, working across mobile and web.
summary: WhatsApp/Slack: real-time 1:1 and group messaging with delivery guarantees.

title: Design a News Feed
coreEntities: Post { id, author_id, body, media_url, created_at }
Feed { user_id → ordered list of post_ids } (materialized)

deepDives.title: Push vs pull vs hybrid
deepDives.content: Push (fan-out on write): precompute each user's feed → O(1) reads, but a celebrity post triggers millions of writes and wastes work on inactive users. Pull (fan-out on read): cheap writes, expensive reads that must merge many timelines. Hybrid: push for the bulk of users; for high-follower accounts, don't fan out, merge their latest posts into the feed at read time. This bounds both write amplification and read latency.

deepDives.title: Feed storage & ranking
deepDives.content: Store each user's feed as a capped list of post_ids in Redis (e.g. last 500). For ranking (not pure chrono), fetch a candidate set and score by a ranking service (recency, affinity, engagement). Hydrate post_ids → full posts from the post store + CDN at read time.

deepDives.title: The celebrity / hot-key problem
deepDives.content: A user with 100M followers is the reason naive push fails. Detect high-fan-out accounts and switch them to pull. This is the same hot-partition issue as sharding, handle the skewed key specially.

deepDives.title: Consistency
deepDives.content: Feeds are fine being eventually consistent, a post showing up 1-2s late is acceptable, which is what lets us do async fan-out through a queue (Kafka) and precomputation.

estimations: 200M DAU, each loads feed ~10x/day → ~23k feed-reads/sec (spiky, much higher at peak).
~1M posts/hour → a few hundred writes/sec.
Feed reads vastly outnumber writes → optimize reads.
functionalReqs: Create a post.
View a feed of posts from followed accounts, newest/ranked first.
Follow/unfollow accounts.
highLevelDesign: The central decision is fan-out. Fan-out on write (push): when a user posts, push the post_id into each follower's precomputed feed list (in Redis). Reads are then O(1), just read your feed list. Fan-out on read (pull): store posts by author; at read time, gather recent posts from everyone you follow and merge. Push gives fast reads but explodes for celebrities (one post → 100M writes). Pull is cheap to write but slow to read. The standard answer is a hybrid: push for normal users, and for celebrity accounts skip the fan-out and merge their posts in at read time. Posts live in a sharded store (Cassandra by author_id) with media on a CDN.
nonFunctionalReqs: Feed loads fast (< ~200ms), read-optimized.
Highly available; eventual consistency is acceptable (a post can appear a few seconds late).
Scale to hundreds of millions of users and celebrity accounts with 100M+ followers.
problem: Design a news feed (like Twitter/Instagram) that shows a user a chronological/ranked feed of posts from accounts they follow.
summary: Twitter/Instagram feed: aggregate posts from people you follow. Push vs pull fan-out.

title: GPU Memory Hierarchy (SRAM vs HBM)
description: A GPU has registers and shared memory / L1 (SRAM, KBs per SM, very fast) and large HBM (tens of GB, high bandwidth but far slower per access). Most deep-learning kernels are bound by HBM bandwidth, not FLOPs, so the game is minimizing HBM reads/writes.
example: FlashAttention keeps attention tiles in SRAM to avoid materializing the N×N matrix in HBM.
keyPoints: Registers > shared/L1 (SRAM) > L2 > HBM (global) > host RAM, by speed.
Memory coalescing: adjacent threads reading contiguous addresses = one wide transaction.
Arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte) decides compute- vs memory-bound (roofline).
summary: On-chip SRAM is tiny but ~10× faster than HBM; most GPU kernels are memory-bound, so data movement dominates.
tradeoffs: SRAM is scarce, tiling trades recompute for fewer HBM trips.
Uncoalesced access can cut effective bandwidth by 10×+.
whenToUse: Reasoning about any GPU kernel's performance; explaining why FlashAttention/kernel-fusion help.

title: Kernel Fusion
description: Each separate GPU kernel reads its inputs from HBM and writes outputs back. Fusing elementwise/reduction ops (e.g. matmul+bias+GELU) into a single kernel keeps intermediate tensors on-chip, eliminating HBM traffic and kernel-launch overhead.
keyPoints: Turns several memory-bound passes into one.
Compilers/torch.compile, Triton, and XLA do this automatically.
Biggest win for elementwise chains and attention.
summary: Combine multiple ops into one kernel so intermediates stay in registers/SRAM instead of round-tripping to HBM.
tradeoffs: Fused kernels are harder to write/debug.
Limited by SRAM capacity for intermediates.
whenToUse: Memory-bound op chains; inference latency optimization.

title: Parallelism: Data vs Model vs Tensor vs Pipeline
description: Data parallelism replicates the model and splits the batch (all-reduce gradients). Model/tensor parallelism splits a single layer's weights across GPUs (splits the matmul, needs all-reduce within each layer). Pipeline parallelism splits layers into stages across GPUs (micro-batches to keep stages busy). Large models combine all three ("3D parallelism").
example: A 70B LLM: tensor-parallel within a node (NVLink) + pipeline across nodes + data-parallel replicas.
keyPoints: Data parallel: simplest, but each GPU must hold the whole model.
Tensor parallel: fits big layers, heavy intra-layer communication (needs NVLink).
Pipeline parallel: fits deep models, watch the "bubble" idle time.
ZeRO/FSDP shards optimizer/grads/params to cut memory.
summary: Four ways to split training/inference across GPUs, each trades compute, memory, and communication differently.
tradeoffs: More splitting = more communication overhead.
Tensor parallel wants fast interconnect; pipeline wants many micro-batches.
whenToUse: When a model or its activations don't fit on one GPU.

title: KV Cache
description: In autoregressive decoding, each new token attends to all previous tokens. Recomputing K/V for the whole prefix every step is wasteful; the KV cache stores per-layer K and V for past tokens so each decode step only computes K/V for the new token. This is the single biggest inference speedup, but the cache grows with sequence length and batch, dominating GPU memory.
keyPoints: Decode step cost drops from O(n²) to O(n) with the cache.
KV cache size = 2 × layers × heads × head_dim × seq_len × batch × dtype, often GBs.
Memory for the KV cache, not compute, usually limits inference batch size.
summary: Cache attention keys/values for past tokens so each decode step is O(n) over the context, instead of O(n^2) from recomputing the whole prefix each step.
tradeoffs: Huge memory footprint; fragmentation wastes it (see PagedAttention).
Long contexts blow up the cache.
whenToUse: Any transformer decoding; central to inference-serving design.

title: Continuous (In-flight) Batching
description: Static batching wastes the GPU because requests finish at different lengths, short ones idle waiting for the longest. Continuous batching (a.k.a. iteration-level scheduling, from Orca) schedules at the token level: as soon as a sequence finishes, a queued request takes its slot, keeping GPU utilization high.
keyPoints: Dramatically higher throughput than static batching under mixed lengths.
Implemented in vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM.
Pairs with PagedAttention for memory management.
summary: Add/remove requests from the running batch every step instead of waiting for the whole batch to finish.
tradeoffs: Scheduler complexity; fairness/latency trade-offs across requests.
whenToUse: High-throughput multi-tenant LLM serving.

title: PagedAttention / vLLM
description: Contiguous KV-cache allocation wastes memory to internal/external fragmentation (you reserve for max length). PagedAttention stores the KV cache in non-contiguous fixed-size blocks with a block table per sequence, like OS paging, cutting waste to <4% and enabling copy-on-write sharing of a common prefix across requests.
keyPoints: Near-zero KV memory waste → much larger effective batch → higher throughput.
Prefix sharing (e.g. a common system prompt) via copy-on-write blocks.
The core idea behind vLLM.
summary: Manage the KV cache in fixed-size pages (like virtual memory) to eliminate fragmentation and enable sharing.
tradeoffs: Custom attention kernel needed to gather non-contiguous blocks.
whenToUse: Production LLM serving where KV memory is the bottleneck.

title: FlashAttention
description: Standard attention writes the full N×N score matrix to HBM (O(N²) memory + bandwidth). FlashAttention computes attention block-by-block in SRAM using online softmax, so it's exact but uses O(N) memory and far less HBM traffic, a big speedup and enabler of longer contexts.
keyPoints: IO-aware: optimizes HBM reads/writes, not just FLOPs.
Online (streaming) softmax avoids storing the full matrix.
Exact (not an approximation).
summary: An IO-aware exact attention kernel that tiles in SRAM and never materializes the N×N matrix in HBM.
tradeoffs: Hand-tuned kernel per hardware generation.
whenToUse: Training and inference of long-context transformers.

title: Quantization (INT8 / FP8 / GPTQ / AWQ)
description: Quantization maps FP16/BF16 values to fewer bits (INT8, INT4, FP8). Since inference is memory-bound, smaller weights mean less HBM traffic and larger batches. Weight-only methods (GPTQ, AWQ) quantize weights to 4-bit with minimal quality loss; FP8 (on Hopper/Blackwell) also speeds compute.
keyPoints: Halving precision ≈ halves memory and bandwidth pressure.
Weight-only 4-bit (GPTQ/AWQ) is popular for LLM serving.
Watch accuracy on outlier activations (per-channel/group scaling helps).
summary: Store/compute weights (and sometimes activations) in lower precision to cut memory and boost throughput.
tradeoffs: Possible quality degradation; calibration needed.
Activation quantization is harder than weight-only.
whenToUse: Fitting bigger models / bigger batches on limited GPU memory.

title: Speculative Decoding
description: Decoding is sequential and latency-bound. Speculative decoding uses a cheap draft model to guess the next k tokens, then the large target model verifies all k in a single forward pass, accepting the longest correct prefix. It preserves the target model's exact output distribution while cutting latency 2-3×.
keyPoints: Trades extra compute for fewer sequential steps.
Output is identical in distribution to the target model.
Draft quality (acceptance rate) drives the speedup.
summary: A small draft model proposes several tokens; the big model verifies them in one parallel pass.
tradeoffs: Needs a good, aligned draft model; wasted work on rejects.
whenToUse: Latency-sensitive LLM serving with spare compute.

title: Prefill vs Decode (and why they differ)
description: Inference has two phases. Prefill runs the full prompt through the model at once, highly parallel and compute-bound, filling the KV cache. Decode then emits tokens one by one, each step is small and memory-bandwidth-bound (reads all weights + KV cache to make one token). They have opposite bottlenecks, so serving systems often schedule/disaggregate them separately.
keyPoints: Prefill: parallel, compute-bound, one big pass.
Decode: sequential, memory-bound, many tiny passes.
Disaggregated prefill/decode (separate pools) is a modern optimization.
summary: Prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel (compute-bound); decode generates one token at a time (memory-bound).
tradeoffs: Mixing both in one batch can hurt latency (chunked prefill helps).
whenToUse: Designing an inference scheduler / capacity planning.

title: Distributed Training: Checkpointing & Recovery
description: Training a large model for weeks across thousands of GPUs will hit hardware failures. Checkpointing periodically saves model + optimizer state so a failure only loses the work since the last checkpoint. Async/sharded checkpointing avoids stalling all GPUs while writing.
keyPoints: Checkpoint = model + optimizer + RNG/step state.
Async & sharded checkpointing minimize the stall.
Elastic training can continue with fewer nodes after a failure.
summary: Long multi-GPU jobs fail often, so periodic checkpoints let you resume instead of restarting.
tradeoffs: Checkpoint frequency: too often wastes I/O, too rare loses work.
Checkpoints of huge models are large, shard across nodes.
whenToUse: Any long-running distributed training job.

title: Design an LLM Inference Service
apiDesign: POST /v1/completions { model, prompt, max_tokens, stream } → SSE token stream

deepDives.title: Batching & scheduling
deepDives.content: Use continuous batching (Orca) so finished sequences free slots immediately, far higher utilization than static batching under mixed lengths. Chunked prefill interleaves prompt processing with decode to protect inter-token latency.

deepDives.title: KV cache memory
deepDives.content: The KV cache dominates memory and limits concurrency. PagedAttention stores it in fixed blocks (no fragmentation) and shares a common prefix (system prompt) via copy-on-write, multiplying effective batch size.

deepDives.title: Scaling & sharding
deepDives.content: Tensor-parallel a big model across GPUs on one node (NVLink); replicate nodes for throughput behind a load balancer. Autoscale on queue depth + GPU util. Route by model and by prefix affinity to reuse KV cache.

deepDives.title: Latency levers
deepDives.content: Quantization (less HBM traffic), speculative decoding (fewer sequential steps), FlashAttention (fast exact attention), and prefill/decode disaggregation all cut latency. Measure TTFT and TPOT separately.

estimations: KV cache/req ≈ 2·layers·heads·head_dim·seq·dtype → often 100s of MB-GBs; it, not FLOPs, caps batch size.
A GPU serves N concurrent sequences bounded by (GPU memory − weights) / KV-per-seq.
functionalReqs: Accept a prompt (+ params) and stream generated tokens back.
Support many concurrent requests of varying prompt/output lengths.
Optional: multiple models, function calling, structured output.
highLevelDesign: Client → API gateway → a request queue → an inference scheduler that runs continuous (in-flight) batching over one or more model-worker replicas. Each replica holds the model (tensor-parallel across GPUs within a node) and a paged KV cache (PagedAttention) to pack many sequences with minimal waste. The scheduler adds/evicts sequences per decode step to keep GPUs busy, streams tokens back over SSE/WebSocket, and an autoscaler adds replicas based on queue depth / GPU utilization. Weights are quantized (e.g. FP8/INT4) to fit bigger batches. Consider disaggregating prefill and decode into separate pools since they're compute- vs memory-bound.
nonFunctionalReqs: Low time-to-first-token and inter-token latency.
High GPU utilization / throughput (cost per token matters).
Highly available and horizontally scalable; graceful under load spikes.
problem: Design a service (like the OpenAI API or a hosted vLLM) that serves token generation from a large language model to many concurrent users with low latency and high GPU efficiency.
summary: Serve a large language model with high throughput and low latency, the modern AI-infra design question.

title: Design a Distributed Model Training Platform
apiDesign: POST /jobs { image, data, gpus, strategy } → job_id

deepDives.title: Choosing parallelism
deepDives.content: Data-parallel when the model fits per GPU; add tensor-parallel (intra-node, NVLink) when a layer is too big; add pipeline-parallel across nodes for very deep models; shard optimizer/params with ZeRO/FSDP to cut memory. Communication cost grows with splitting.

deepDives.title: Fault tolerance
deepDives.content: Gang scheduling + frequent sharded checkpoints + elastic restart. Detect stragglers/dead nodes via heartbeats and reschedule. The all-reduce ring must be rebuilt on membership change.

deepDives.title: Utilization
deepDives.content: Overlap communication with computation, use gradient accumulation for large effective batches, and bin-pack jobs. Pipeline "bubbles" waste GPUs, tune micro-batch count.

estimations: Weeks-long jobs on 1000s of GPUs → failures are frequent → checkpoint cadence matters.
Interconnect bandwidth (NVLink/InfiniBand) bounds parallelism strategy.
functionalReqs: Submit a job (code, data, resources); schedule it onto GPUs.
Support data/tensor/pipeline parallelism and checkpointing.
Monitor metrics, logs, and resume failed jobs.
highLevelDesign: A control plane accepts jobs and a gang scheduler places all workers of a job together (they must run simultaneously). Workers run the training loop with a parallelism strategy: data-parallel (all-reduce gradients each step, e.g. via NCCL), plus tensor/pipeline parallelism and ZeRO/FSDP sharding for models too big for one GPU. Periodic sharded, async checkpoints go to object storage so a failed job resumes from the last checkpoint (elastic training can proceed with fewer nodes). A metrics/logging pipeline tracks loss/throughput.
nonFunctionalReqs: High GPU utilization across the cluster.
Fault tolerance, a node failure shouldn't restart from scratch.
Fair multi-tenant scheduling.
patterns: Parallelism: Data vs Model vs Tensor vs Pipeline
problem: Design a platform that lets ML engineers run large-scale distributed training jobs across a GPU cluster, efficiently and with recovery from failures.
summary: Train large models across thousands of GPUs reliably, scheduling, parallelism, fault tolerance.

title: Design a Recommendation / Ranking System

deepDives.title: Two-stage retrieval + ranking
deepDives.content: Retrieval (recall-oriented, cheap, ANN over embeddings) narrows millions → hundreds; ranking (precision-oriented, feature-rich model) orders them. This is the standard way to make big-catalog recs tractable in latency budget.

deepDives.title: Feature store & freshness
deepDives.content: Serve features from a fast store (Redis/DynamoDB) with online (streaming) updates for recent behavior plus batch features. Watch train/serve skew, compute features the same way in both paths.

deepDives.title: Training loop & feedback
deepDives.content: Log impressions + labels (clicks/watch time), retrain regularly, and guard against feedback loops/position bias. A/B test model changes.

estimations: Can't score millions of items per request → two-stage: cheap retrieval then expensive ranking of ~hundreds.
functionalReqs: Given a user + context, return a ranked list of items.
Incorporate fresh signals (recent interactions).
Log impressions/engagement for training.
highLevelDesign: Two stages: (1) Candidate generation retrieves a few hundred plausible items from millions via approximate nearest-neighbor search over learned embeddings (two-tower model). (2) A heavier ranking model scores those candidates using user/item/context features fetched from a low-latency feature store. Results are re-ranked for diversity/business rules and returned. An offline pipeline logs impressions + engagement and continuously retrains models; features are computed in both batch and streaming (online) for freshness. Cache embeddings and precompute where possible.
nonFunctionalReqs: Low serving latency (<~200ms) at high QPS.
Handle huge item catalogs and cold start.
Continuously retrain on fresh engagement data.
problem: Design the ML system behind a personalized feed/recommendations (e.g. video or product recs) that returns ranked items in real time.
summary: Serve personalized ranked results at scale, candidate generation → ranking → serving.

description: DNS resolves a hostname (api.example.com) to an IP. A recursive resolver walks the hierarchy (root, TLD, authoritative) and caches results by TTL. It also doubles as a coarse load-balancing and failover layer: return different IPs by geography (GeoDNS), round-robin across servers, or fail over by updating records.
example: Route 53 latency-based routing sends EU users to eu-west, US users to us-east.
keyPoints: Resolution: recursive resolver, root, TLD, authoritative nameserver, cached by TTL.
Record types: A/AAAA (IP), CNAME (alias), NS, MX, TXT.
TTL trades freshness vs load: low TTL = faster failover but more lookups.
GeoDNS / latency-based routing sends users to the nearest region.
DNS round-robin is cheap load balancing but ignores server health.
summary: Turn a domain name into an IP address, the first hop of almost every request.
tradeoffs: Low TTL enables fast failover but increases query load and cost.
DNS-level LB cannot see server health or do sticky sessions.
whenToUse: Every internet-facing system; multi-region routing and coarse failover.
title: DNS

description: A reverse proxy sits in front of servers and forwards requests to them (nginx, Envoy). An API gateway is a reverse proxy specialized for APIs: routing, auth, rate limiting, request/response transformation, and response aggregation for microservices. A load balancer spreads load; a reverse proxy/gateway adds cross-cutting concerns.
keyPoints: Reverse proxy: TLS termination, compression, caching, hides backend topology.
API gateway adds auth, rate limiting, routing, and aggregation across microservices.
Load balancer vs reverse proxy: LB spreads load, reverse proxy adds features (they overlap).
Centralizing auth and rate-limiting at the edge keeps individual services simple.
The gateway is on the critical path, run it redundantly so it is not a bottleneck/SPOF.
summary: A single front door that routes, terminates TLS, authenticates, and rate-limits before traffic reaches your services.
tradeoffs: Centralized cross-cutting logic vs an extra hop and a component to scale/secure.
Gateway can become a bottleneck; keep per-request work light.
whenToUse: Microservices, public APIs, anywhere you need edge auth/rate-limiting/routing.
title: Reverse Proxy & API Gateway

description: Microservices break a monolith into small, independently deployable services owned by small teams. They scale and deploy independently but add network calls, partial failures, and ops overhead. Service discovery lets services locate each other without hardcoded IPs via a registry (Consul/etcd), with client-side or server-side discovery, often through a service-mesh sidecar (Envoy).
keyPoints: Monolith: simple to build and deploy, but scaling and team autonomy suffer at size.
Microservices: independent deploy/scale/ownership, at the cost of network calls and ops complexity.
Service discovery: a registry maps service name to healthy instances.
Client-side (client picks instance) vs server-side (LB/gateway picks) discovery.
Service mesh (sidecar proxies) handles discovery, retries, mTLS, and observability uniformly.
summary: Split a system into independently deployable services, and let them find each other dynamically.
tradeoffs: Independent scaling/deploys vs distributed-systems complexity (partial failure, tracing, data consistency).
Do not start with microservices, extract them when the monolith actually hurts.
whenToUse: Large orgs/codebases where independent deployment and team autonomy outweigh the added complexity.
title: Microservices & Service Discovery

description: REST uses HTTP verbs over resources, simple, cacheable, ubiquitous. gRPC uses HTTP/2 + protobuf for fast, strongly-typed, streaming service-to-service calls. GraphQL exposes a single endpoint where clients ask for exactly the fields they need, killing over/under-fetching but complicating caching and rate-limiting.
keyPoints: REST: stateless resource + verb, HTTP caching, universal, but can over/under-fetch.
gRPC: HTTP/2 + protobuf (compact, typed), bidirectional streaming, great for internal service-to-service.
GraphQL: one endpoint, client picks fields, avoids over/under-fetch, harder to cache and rate-limit.
Use REST for public/simple APIs, gRPC for internal high-throughput, GraphQL for client-driven data.
Also: WebSockets/SSE for push, webhooks for server-to-server events.
summary: How services talk: resource-based REST, high-performance gRPC, or flexible GraphQL.
tradeoffs: gRPC is fast and typed but not browser-native (needs a proxy) and less human-debuggable.
GraphQL flexibility complicates caching, auth, and query-cost control (N+1).
whenToUse: Choosing the transport between clients and services, or between services.
title: API Paradigms: REST vs gRPC vs GraphQL

description: TCP is connection-oriented, reliable, ordered (handshake, retransmits, congestion control), used by HTTP and most apps. UDP is connectionless, fast, and lossy, used for video/voice/gaming/DNS where speed beats reliability. HTTP/1.1 is text with one in-flight request per connection, HTTP/2 multiplexes streams, HTTP/3 runs over QUIC (UDP) to avoid head-of-line blocking.
keyPoints: TCP: reliable, ordered, congestion-controlled; the 3-way handshake adds latency.
UDP: no handshake or guarantees, minimal overhead; the app handles loss (video, VoIP, gaming, DNS).
HTTP/1.1: head-of-line blocking, one in-flight request per connection (keep-alive helps).
HTTP/2: multiplexed streams over one TCP connection, header compression.
HTTP/3: QUIC over UDP removes TCP head-of-line blocking and speeds up connection setup.
summary: Reliable ordered TCP vs fast lossy UDP, and how HTTP evolved on top.
tradeoffs: TCP reliability costs latency (handshake, retransmits); UDP is fast but you own loss/ordering.
HTTP/2 still suffers TCP-level HOL blocking; HTTP/3 fixes it via UDP.
whenToUse: Reasoning about latency, real-time media, or protocol choice for a service.
title: Networking: TCP, UDP & HTTP

description: For live data (chat, notifications, feeds) you need server-to-client push. Short polling repeatedly asks (simple, wasteful). Long polling holds the request open until there is data. SSE is a one-way server-to-client stream over HTTP. WebSockets are a persistent full-duplex connection, best for bidirectional real-time.
keyPoints: Short polling: client asks every N seconds, simple but wasteful and laggy.
Long polling: server holds the request until data or timeout, near-real-time over plain HTTP.
SSE: one-way server-to-client event stream with auto-reconnect, great for feeds/notifications.
WebSockets: persistent full-duplex, best for chat/multiplayer/collab; needs sticky sessions or a pub/sub backplane.
At scale, fan-out via a pub/sub layer (Redis/Kafka) so any server can push to any client.
summary: Push updates to clients: polling, long-polling, SSE, or full-duplex WebSockets.
tradeoffs: WebSockets give true bidirectional push but are stateful (connection affinity, harder to scale/LB).
Polling is simple and stateless but wastes requests and adds latency.
whenToUse: Chat, live feeds, notifications, dashboards, collaborative editing, multiplayer.
title: Real-time: WebSockets, SSE & Polling

description: Object storage (S3, GCS) stores files as immutable objects in a flat key namespace with metadata, accessed by key over HTTP. It is cheap, durable (replicated), and effectively infinite, but not for low-latency random updates. Do not store big blobs in your DB, put them in object storage and keep a URL/pointer in the DB. Use presigned URLs so clients upload/download directly.
keyPoints: Objects are immutable; an update writes a new version. Flat key namespace, not a filesystem.
Cheap, durable (multi-AZ replication), and near-infinite capacity.
Store the file in object storage, keep only the key/URL in your database.
Presigned URLs let clients upload/download directly, offloading your servers.
Put a CDN in front for hot public assets.
summary: Store large immutable files (images, video, backups) cheaply, and serve them via CDN.
tradeoffs: Great for large immutable blobs; bad for low-latency small random writes or transactions.
Listing and overwrite consistency can be eventual in some systems.
whenToUse: Images, video, file uploads, backups, static assets, data-lake storage.
title: Object / Blob Storage

description: B-trees (Postgres, InnoDB) update pages in place, giving fast reads and good range scans but random-write cost and write amplification. LSM-trees (Cassandra, RocksDB) batch writes in memory then flush sorted files (SSTables) merged by background compaction, giving high write throughput at the cost of read amplification (softened by Bloom filters) and compaction overhead. A write-ahead log (WAL) makes both durable.
keyPoints: B-tree: in-place page updates, excellent reads and range queries, moderate write cost.
LSM-tree: memtable, then immutable SSTables + compaction, excellent write throughput.
LSM reads may touch several SSTables; Bloom filters skip files that cannot contain the key.
WAL (write-ahead log): append every change first so a crash can recover.
Rule of thumb: read-heavy/OLTP prefers B-tree; write-heavy/time-series/logs prefer LSM.
summary: How databases physically store data: read-optimized B-trees vs write-optimized LSM-trees.
tradeoffs: B-tree: better reads, worse random-write throughput and write amplification.
LSM: better writes, but read amplification and background compaction (CPU/IO spikes).
whenToUse: Choosing or reasoning about a database write/read profile.
title: Storage Engines: B-Tree vs LSM-Tree

description: Networks fail mid-request, so clients retry, which can double-charge or double-create. An idempotent operation can be applied multiple times without changing the result beyond the first. Combine at-least-once delivery with idempotency to get effectively-exactly-once. Implement with an idempotency key: store the key and its result, and on a duplicate return the stored result instead of re-executing.
keyPoints: GET/PUT/DELETE are naturally idempotent; POST usually is not.
Client sends an idempotency key; the server dedups on it and returns the first result.
At-least-once delivery + idempotent handlers = effectively-once, without exactly-once cost.
Essential for payments, order creation, and any queue consumer (messages redeliver).
Store keys with a TTL and scope them to the operation + inputs.
summary: Make retried requests safe: applying the same operation twice has the same effect as once.
tradeoffs: Requires storing keys/results (state + cleanup) but eliminates duplicate side effects.
True exactly-once end-to-end is very hard; idempotency is the practical substitute.
whenToUse: Payments, order/booking creation, webhook handlers, any message-queue consumer.
title: Idempotency

description: When a business action spans multiple services/databases you cannot use one ACID transaction. Two-phase commit (2PC) has a coordinator prepare then commit all participants, atomic but blocking and a coordinator SPOF. Sagas break the action into local transactions, each with a compensating action to undo on failure, coordinated by choreography (events) or orchestration (a central saga). The outbox pattern reliably publishes events with the local commit.
keyPoints: 2PC: prepare then commit across participants; atomic but blocks and stalls if the coordinator dies.
Saga: a sequence of local transactions plus compensating transactions to roll back.
Choreography (services react to events) vs orchestration (a central coordinator drives steps).
Sagas give eventual consistency, not isolation, design for intermediate states.
Outbox pattern: write the event to an outbox table in the same local transaction, then publish.
summary: Keep data consistent across services without one database: two-phase commit or sagas.
tradeoffs: 2PC gives atomicity but is blocking, slow, and does not scale across many services.
Sagas scale and stay available but are eventually consistent and add compensation complexity.
whenToUse: A workflow spanning multiple services/databases (order, payment, inventory, shipping).
title: Distributed Transactions: 2PC & Saga

description: Distributed systems must agree on things (who is the leader, what is committed) despite crashes and partitions. Consensus algorithms (Raft, Paxos) elect a leader and replicate a log so a majority (quorum) agrees. Coordination services (ZooKeeper, etcd) provide leader election, distributed locks, and config on top of consensus. Gossip spreads membership peer-to-peer; heartbeats detect failures.
keyPoints: Consensus (Raft/Paxos): a quorum (majority) agrees on an ordered log; survives minority failures.
Leader election: one node coordinates writes; on failure a new leader is elected.
ZooKeeper/etcd: managed leader election, distributed locks, and config (built on consensus).
Gossip protocol: nodes randomly exchange state to spread membership (Cassandra, Dynamo).
Heartbeats + timeouts detect dead nodes; beware split-brain (use quorum/fencing).
summary: Get a cluster to agree on a value/leader despite failures: Raft/Paxos, ZooKeeper, leader election.
tradeoffs: Quorum consistency costs latency (round-trips) and availability if you lose the majority.
More replicas = more fault tolerance but slower writes (wait for quorum).
whenToUse: Leader election, distributed locks, config/service discovery, replicated logs.
title: Consensus & Coordination

description: When exact tracking is too big for memory, probabilistic structures trade a little accuracy for massive space savings. A Bloom filter tests set membership with no false negatives but some false positives, great to skip expensive lookups. HyperLogLog estimates cardinality (unique counts) in kilobytes. Count-Min Sketch estimates item frequencies (heavy hitters).
keyPoints: Bloom filter: definitely-not-present or maybe-present, no false negatives, small and fast.
Used to skip disk/DB lookups (LSM SSTables, caches, have-I-seen-this-URL).
HyperLogLog: count unique items (e.g. unique visitors) in ~KB with ~2% error.
Count-Min Sketch: approximate frequencies / top-K heavy hitters in fixed memory.
You can add to a standard Bloom filter but not remove (use a counting variant).
summary: Tiny, approximate structures that answer membership/cardinality/frequency at huge scale.
tradeoffs: Huge memory savings vs a controlled false-positive rate (tune bits and hashes).
Approximate, not exact; unsuitable when a wrong answer is unacceptable.
whenToUse: Dedup at scale, cache/DB lookup skipping, unique counts, heavy-hitter detection.
title: Bloom Filters & Probabilistic Structures

description: Availability is the percent of time a system serves requests, measured in nines (99.9% is ~8.7h/yr down, 99.99% ~52min). You reach it with redundancy and fast failover. Active-passive keeps a standby that takes over on failure; active-active runs all nodes live behind a load balancer (more capacity, harder state). Health checks detect failures; eliminate single points of failure.
keyPoints: Nines: 99.9% is ~8.7h/yr, 99.99% ~52min/yr, 99.999% ~5min/yr of downtime.
Redundancy everywhere: no single point of failure (multi-AZ, multi-instance).
Active-passive: a standby is promoted on failover (simpler, wasted capacity).
Active-active: all nodes serve traffic (more capacity, needs shared/replicated state).
Health checks + automated failover; track MTBF (between failures) and MTTR (to recover).
summary: Design for uptime: redundancy, the nines, active-passive vs active-active, health checks.
tradeoffs: Higher availability means more redundancy and cost; each extra nine is much harder.
Availability vs consistency during partitions (see CAP).
whenToUse: Setting SLAs and failure behavior for any production service.
title: Availability & Failover

description: Security is a design concern, not an afterthought. Encrypt in transit (TLS/HTTPS) and at rest. Authenticate users (sessions, JWT, OAuth2/OIDC) and authorize every action (RBAC, least privilege). Validate and sanitize all input (SQLi, XSS). Protect against abuse (rate limiting, WAF, DDoS). Keep secrets in a vault, never in code.
keyPoints: Encrypt in transit (TLS) and at rest; terminate TLS at the edge/gateway.
AuthN vs AuthZ: verify identity (JWT/sessions/OAuth2/OIDC) then check permissions (RBAC, least privilege).
Validate/sanitize all input; use parameterized queries (SQLi) and escape output (XSS).
Rate limiting + WAF + DDoS protection at the edge; add CSRF protection for cookie auth.
Store secrets in a manager/vault, rotate keys, never commit credentials.
summary: The baseline: TLS everywhere, real authn/authz, encryption, least privilege, and abuse protection.
tradeoffs: Stateless JWTs scale but are hard to revoke before expiry; sessions revoke easily but need a store.
Security controls add latency/friction; balance against the threat model.
whenToUse: Every system handling user data, auth, payments, or public exposure.
title: Security Essentials

description: Observability is how you understand a running system. Logs are discrete events, metrics are numeric time series (cheap, aggregatable), traces follow one request across services. Alert on symptoms users feel (the four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation), not every cause. Define SLIs/SLOs and an error budget to balance reliability vs velocity.
keyPoints: Three pillars: logs (events), metrics (time series), traces (a request across services).
Four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation, alert on these.
RED (rate, errors, duration) for services; USE (utilization, saturation, errors) for resources.
Distributed tracing (trace/span IDs) pinpoints which hop is slow in microservices.
SLI/SLO/SLA + error budget: measure reliability and decide when to slow features.
summary: See what production is doing: the three pillars, golden signals, and SLOs.
tradeoffs: More telemetry means faster debugging but storage cost and cardinality blow-ups (watch high-cardinality labels).
Alert on symptoms, not causes, to avoid pager fatigue.
whenToUse: Any production service, especially microservices where failures are non-obvious.
title: Observability: Logs, Metrics & Traces

coreEntities: Trie node { char, children, cached top-K }

deepDives.title: Fast prefix lookup
deepDives.content: A trie gives O(len(prefix)) traversal. Store precomputed top-K suggestions at each node so you never scan the subtree per request. Rebuild top-K in batch when frequencies change.

deepDives.title: Ranking & freshness
deepDives.content: Rank by historical frequency plus recency/personalization. Trending terms come from a streaming layer (Count-Min Sketch for heavy hitters) merged into the trie on a schedule; full rebuilds run offline from query logs.

deepDives.title: Scale & latency
deepDives.content: Shard the trie by first character/prefix across nodes and replicate for read scale. Cache hot prefixes in Redis/CDN. Debounce keystrokes client-side (50-100ms) to cut QPS.

estimations: Billions of queries/day, every keystroke is a request, so very high QPS.
K is small (5-10); top-K precomputed per node.
functionalReqs: Return top-K suggestions for a given prefix.
Update on every keystroke with low latency.
Rank by popularity/recency.
highLevelDesign: Build a trie (prefix tree) of terms and precompute/cache the top-K completions at each node so a lookup is O(prefix length). Serve from an in-memory service sharded by prefix, fronted by a cache/CDN. A separate offline pipeline aggregates query logs into term frequencies and rebuilds the trie periodically. Debounce keystrokes on the client and cache recent prefixes.
nonFunctionalReqs: Very low latency (<100ms) per keystroke.
Read-heavy, high QPS.
Millions of terms; suggestions can be slightly stale.
problem: Design search autocomplete that suggests the top completions for a prefix on every keystroke.
summary: Suggest the top completions as a user types each character, like a search box.
title: Design a Typeahead / Autocomplete

apiDesign: POST /notifications { user_id, type, payload } -> { id, status }
coreEntities: Notification { id, user_id, channel, template, payload, status }

deepDives.title: Reliability & retries
deepDives.content: Providers fail and rate-limit. Queue everything; workers retry with exponential backoff and route poison messages to a DLQ. Idempotency keys make redelivery safe (at-least-once + idempotent = no dupes). Track per-message status.

deepDives.title: Fan-out at scale
deepDives.content: Notify 10M followers cannot be synchronous. Enqueue a fan-out job that batches recipients into per-user messages across workers, rate-limited per provider and per user (respect quiet hours + preferences).

deepDives.title: Preferences & dedup
deepDives.content: Check opt-outs and channel prefs before sending. De-dup identical notifications within a window, coalesce bursts (do not send five liked-your-post alerts in a minute).

estimations: Millions of notifications/day with event spikes.
Bursty fan-out; size worker pools and queues for peak.
functionalReqs: Send via multiple channels (push/email/SMS).
Support transactional and bulk/fan-out notifications.
Respect user preferences and de-duplicate.
highLevelDesign: A service accepts requests and enqueues them (Kafka/queue). Per-channel workers pull from the queue, render templates, check preferences/opt-outs, and call provider adapters (APNs/FCM, SES, Twilio) with retries and rate limiting. Idempotency keys avoid duplicates on retry; a dead-letter queue captures failures. Fan-out (notify all followers) expands to per-user messages asynchronously.
nonFunctionalReqs: High throughput and reliable (at-least-once) delivery.
Tolerate third-party provider failures/rate limits.
Low latency for transactional; bulk can be async.
problem: Design a system that sends notifications to users across push, email, and SMS (order updates, social alerts).
summary: Deliver notifications across push, email, and SMS reliably and at scale.
title: Design a Notification System

deepDives.title: Snowflake bit layout
deepDives.content: e.g. 41 bits timestamp (~69 years), 10 bits machine id (1024 nodes), 12 bits sequence (4096 ids/ms/node). No cross-node coordination; the machine id (from ZooKeeper/config) prevents collisions.

deepDives.title: Clock skew & ordering
deepDives.content: IDs are only as ordered as clocks. Handle backward clock jumps (wait or refuse) to avoid duplicates, and NTP-sync nodes. Rough (k-)ordering is usually enough; strict global order needs a single sequencer.

deepDives.title: Alternatives & tradeoffs
deepDives.content: UUIDv4: trivial, no coordination, but 128-bit and not sortable (poor DB index locality). DB auto-increment/ticket server: sortable but a SPOF/bottleneck unless you allocate ranges. Snowflake balances both.

estimations: Millions of ids/sec across the fleet; 4096 ids/ms/node.
64-bit fits a DB bigint and indexes well.
functionalReqs: Generate globally unique IDs.
IDs are roughly sortable by time (k-ordered).
High throughput, no central bottleneck.
highLevelDesign: Use the Snowflake approach: a 64-bit ID = timestamp (ms since a custom epoch) + machine/worker id + a per-ms sequence counter. Each node generates IDs locally with no coordination, guaranteeing uniqueness (unique machine id) and rough time-ordering (high timestamp bits). Alternatives: UUIDv4 (random, unique, not sortable, 128-bit) or a ticket server / DB range allocation (each server pre-allocates a block of ids).
nonFunctionalReqs: Very high QPS, low latency.
No collisions even across data centers.
Highly available (no SPOF).
problem: Design a service that generates unique, roughly time-ordered 64-bit IDs across many machines, like Twitter Snowflake.
summary: Generate unique, roughly time-ordered 64-bit IDs across many machines (Snowflake).
title: Design a Distributed Unique ID Generator

deepDives.title: Dedup at billions of URLs
deepDives.content: An exact seen-set of billions of URLs is too big for memory. Use a Bloom filter (no false negatives) to skip already-seen URLs cheaply, backed by a durable store. Canonicalize URLs before checking.

deepDives.title: Politeness & the frontier
deepDives.content: Partition the frontier by hostname so one worker handles a host with a rate limit (crawl-delay), avoiding DoSing sites. Prioritize by importance/freshness and honor robots.txt (cached per host).

deepDives.title: Scale & fault tolerance
deepDives.content: Distribute fetchers/parsers and store the frontier durably (Kafka/DB) so a crash resumes. Detect traps (infinite calendars, session ids) with URL/pattern limits. Store content in object storage, index offline.

estimations: Billions of pages, ~100KB avg, so petabytes of storage.
Throughput = pages/sec x workers, bounded by per-host politeness.
functionalReqs: Fetch pages from seeds, following links (BFS).
Avoid re-crawling the same URL; respect robots.txt.
Extract text/links and store content.
highLevelDesign: A URL frontier feeds fetcher workers that download pages; a parser extracts text + links; new links are normalized, deduped against a seen-set, and enqueued. Raw pages go to object storage, metadata to a DB. Politeness: partition the frontier by host with per-host rate limits and honor robots.txt/crawl-delay. Dedup URLs with a Bloom filter (billions will not fit exact in memory). Distribute fetchers and make the frontier durable so crawls resume.
nonFunctionalReqs: Scale to billions of pages, high throughput.
Politeness: do not hammer a single host.
Fault-tolerant and resumable.
problem: Design a scalable web crawler that fetches billions of pages for a search index, politely and without re-crawling.
summary: Fetch billions of pages for a search index, politely and without loops.
title: Design a Web Crawler
